content.title: COOKING MISTAKES THAT QUIETLY DRAIN THE NUTRIENTS FROM YOUR MEALS
facts: **Boiling broccoli** – Up to half its vitamin C can leach into the water; steaming for 4-5 minutes keeps far more intact.
**Draining canned beans and tossing the liquid** – That aquafaba holds potassium and soluble fiber; rinse gently instead of dumping it all out.
**Adding olive oil at the very start of cooking** – High heat breaks down its polyphenols fast; drizzle raw oil on at the end for the most benefit.
**Peeling potatoes before boiling** – Most of the fiber and a chunk of the vitamin C sit right under the skin; cook them unpeeled when you can.
**Microwaving vegetables in a lot of water** – It behaves like boiling and washes out nutrients; use a splash of water and a covered dish instead.
**Chopping vegetables long before cooking** – Cut surfaces exposed to air for hours lose vitamin C through oxidation; prep closer to cooking time.
**Overcooking eggs until the yolk turns grey-green** – That's oxidized iron and sulfur; a softer yolk keeps more choline and B-vitamins usable.
**Salting meat right before it hits a hot pan** – It draws out moisture too fast and dries the protein; salt right before cooking or well in advance, not in between.

content.caption:
A few small kitchen habits change how much nutrition actually makes it onto your plate. With broccoli, vitamin C is water-soluble, so the longer it sits submerged in boiling water, the more of it dissolves out and gets poured down the drain. With olive oil, its polyphenols and some of its healthy fat structure start to degrade at high heat, so cooking it low or adding it raw at the end preserves more of what makes it 'healthy' in the first place. And with potatoes, the skin acts like a nutrient barrier — peeling it off before cooking removes fiber and vitamin C that would otherwise stay locked in during boiling. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so start with the swap that feels easiest for you.
